newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore property buoyant despite economy-report.
newsitem.headline: Singapore property buoyant despite economy-report.

text.p: Singapore property investment sales doubled in 1996 to Singapore $12.9 billion despite the economy's second-half slowdown, a report from property consultancy Edmund Tie & Company said on Tuesday.
The company's market overview report said activity was boosted by government land sales, accounting for 40 percent of the year's total.
The report said investment sales would remain stable in 1997 with interest from foreign and local developers in prime sites.

But the report revealed a slowdown in residential investment sales, which accounted for only 47 percent of the year's total against 51 percent in 1995, and a general plateau in the office, retail and industrial sectors.

Average prime rents in the office market dropped between three and nine percent in the fourth quarter of 1996 with new completions totalling 1.6 million sq ft, about half of the 1995 total of 3.1 million sq ft.
Edmund Tie said it expected pressure on rentals in older properties as demand for new office space was healthy, with 30 percent of new supply to be completed in 1997 already committed.

In retail, average rentals fell 10 percent year on year. The market is expected to remain competitive with over two million sq ft completing in 1997, although new interest in retailing in Singapore is expected from foreign firms, said the report.

Industrial rentals eased about five percent over the year, but capital values increased by the same amount. The report said about 6.6 million sq ft was added to the industrial sector in the year with consolidation expected for 1997.
Demand for industrial property was seen high in logistics bases in 1997 thanks to Singapore's position as a regional hub for firms trading across Asia.

On the residential side, the report said a promising start to 1996 saw condominium prices jump between five and 15 percent in the first quarter of the year, but a mid-point consolidation after the government introduced anti-speculation measures saw prices close virtually unchanged at the year end.
The report said 1997 residential values were likely to consolidate further and rentals would come under pressure as new housing stock came onto the market over the next two years.
